title: A child on the throne
hook: Duleep Singh, a small boy, becomes Maharaja, with his mother as regent

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sher Singh and the ministers, and your line was intrigue kills. When a whisper came your way, did you let it stop with you? Today, who was left to sit on the throne. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

A small boy is led to the throne of the Punjab. His feet don't reach the floor from the cushion. Around him stand grown men who have just watched a Maharaja, a prince and a chief minister die, and who now bow to a child. Beside him, watching all of them, sits his mother. The boy is Duleep Singh, the youngest son of Ranjit Singh. The woman is Maharani Jind Kaur. Today: a child on the throne.
screen: `A SMALL BOY LED TO THE THRONE.` → `GROWN MEN BOW TO A CHILD.` → `HIS MOTHER WATCHES THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: First, why a child. After yesterday's killings, the men who held the army needed a Maharaja they could manage. Hira Singh, the dead minister's son, raised the boy Duleep Singh to the throne and ruled as chief minister in his name. A child king is easy to seat on a throne. That was part of the point. Second, the mother. Jind Kaur stood beside her son as regent, and she was no quiet figure. Histories describe her as sharp and strong-willed. Hira Singh did not last long; he too fell in the court's quarrels, and in time her own brother, Jawahar Singh, became chief minister. Third, the danger. A child can't command an army or read a treaty. Everyone around him had a plan for his name. The ministers wanted it to rule by. The army wanted it to fight under. The British, watching from across the river, wanted to know who really held the power. A boy on a throne is a name with many hands reaching for it. Fourth, how the Gurus speak of the small and the protected. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, the Lord is called father and mother, kin and brother, and protector in every place, so what is there to fear? It's the safety a small child feels when someone greater is watching. Duleep Singh had a throne, a mother and a court. What he needed most was someone who wanted nothing from him. That's today's line.
screen: `THE SON WHO WAS LEFT.` · `HIS MOTHER AS REGENT.` · `MANY HANDS REACHING FOR ONE NAME.` · `THE LORD AS FATHER AND MOTHER.` · then, large: `A CHILD KING.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a child. Sit, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind one child you know, or the child you once were. Picture them small, in a room full of grown-ups who are busy and loud. Now picture one adult in that room turning toward them, kneeling down to their height, wanting nothing from them except that they're all right. Stay with that picture. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, holding that child in mind. The bell holds the time.
Duleep Singh, the youngest son of Ranjit Singh, made Maharaja as a small boy, with his mother, Jind Kaur, beside him as regent. Today's word.
Your line: a child king. Today, protect a child in one small way: listen properly, step in, or simply make sure they're safe. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Duleep Singh, enthroned as a child with his mother, Maharani Jind Kaur, as regent, and his story is told in Sikh homes and gurdwaras.

notes: The outline hook gives Duleep Singh's age (five); the voice says only 'a small boy' under the claims rule. Confirm and add the age only with a source.
Other sons of Ranjit Singh (Peshaura Singh, Kashmira Singh) were alive and are not named; confirm the framing that the court chose a child it could manage.
Jind Kaur's characterization and the disputed British accounts of her: please check framing; day 924 covers her separately.
Ang 103 (Majh M5, 'tu mera pita tu hai mera mata') paraphrased; confirm the Ang.

Editor pass: fixed the sequence (Jind Kaur did not push out Hira Singh herself; he fell in the court's quarrels before Jawahar Singh became chief minister), cut the repeat of day 924's British-accounts angle, softened 'runs all through Sikh devotion' and removed the unsourced 'last Maharaja' and 'often told' from howItsDone.

Audit pass: Ranjit Singh's court did not use a crown (he famously refused one), so the hook's 'crown of the Punjab set before a small boy' and 'a crown with many hands' now speak of the throne and the boy's name. The Ang 103 paraphrase said the hymn pictures the one who prays as a child; the hymn (tu mera pita tu hai mera mata, tu mera bandhap tu mera bhrata, tu mera rakha sabhni thai) names father, mother, kin, brother and protector, so the teach and myth reveal now follow it and keep the child picture as the script's own image. Day 924 also says 'wear the crown' (another writer's day); flag for that day's auditor.
